abstract: Cell division is a fundamental biological process underlying plant growth and devel-opment and ensuring the transmission of genetic and epigenetic information. Although cell-cycle regulation has been extensively investigated using suspension-cultured cells and molecular reporters, these experimental systems do not fully reproduce the hor-monal environment, cellular identity, and chromatin organization of cells within intact plant tissues. From a physical perspective, cell-cycle progression also involves sub-stantial structural remodeling of genetic material, particularly during the transition from the G2 nuclear configuration to condensed mitotic chromosomes. The magnitude of this remodeling may depend on the initial geometry and organization of chromatin. Here, we quantitatively characterized nuclear and chromatin architecture in different cell types of the Arabidopsis thaliana root, focusing on the structural differences be-tween G2 and mitotic states. In parallel, we assessed CYCB1 reporter expression using GUS and GFP signal intensities. We found that epidermal and cortical cells exhibited greater G2-to-M structural distances accompanied by higher CYCB1 reporter signals, whereas inner root tissues showed smaller structural distances and lower reporter in-tensities. These findings reveal a relationship between cell-type-specific chromatin architecture and CYCB1 reporter accumulation. We propose that differences in the structural re-modeling required for mitotic entry contribute to the spatial heterogeneity of cell-cycle regulation in plant tissues. Importantly, CYCB1 reporter intensity should not be interpreted as a direct or universal quantitative measure of cell-cycle activity across structurally distinct cell types. Instead, quantitative analysis of nuclear geometry and chromatin organization provides an important complementary approach for investigat-ing the physical requirements of cell-cycle transitions in intact plant tissues.
